title: Notes with backspaces
statement:
Two people typed notes on a keyboard where `#` means backspace: it deletes the character before it, if any. Backspace on an empty note does nothing.

Given the raw keystrokes `a` and `b`, return true if both produce the same final text.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What happens with a backspace on an empty note?
clarifyingQuestions.why: A naive pop on an empty list can crash.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is # the only special character?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, every other character is typed text.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How long are the inputs?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 200 characters each, but think about a constant-space version.

edgeCases.why: Backspaces at the start do nothing.

approaches.name: Build both results with a stack
approaches.idea: Push characters, pop on #, then compare the two results.

approaches.name: Two pointers from the end
approaches.idea: Walk both strings backward, counting pending backspaces to skip characters, and compare the next real character from each.
approaches.tradeoffs: Constant space but trickier to get right.

optimal.name: Stack per note, or reverse two pointers
optimal.explanation: Process each note with a stack: push normal characters, pop on # when the stack is non-empty. Compare the results. For O(1) space, walk from the end of both strings with a skip counter each, and compare the next surviving characters.
optimal.space: O(n + m), or O(1) with two pointers

hintLadder: Which structure naturally removes the most recent item?
Could you avoid building the strings by reading from the end?
Use a stack for each note, or two pointers from the end with a count of backspaces to skip.

expectedMentions.what: Asks what a backspace does on an empty note
Proposes simulating with a stack and states O(n + m)
Mentions the two-pointer O(1) space version

followUps: Do it in O(1) extra space.
Add an undo key that restores the last deleted character.

walkthrough.say: A backspace on an empty note does nothing, right? And hash is the only special character?
The simplest approach is to simulate typing with a stack for each note: push characters, pop on hash. Then compare. That’s linear time and space.
If space mattered, I could walk both strings backward with a counter of backspaces to skip. I’ll start with the stack for clarity and mention that as the follow-up.
A helper that returns the final text. I only pop if there is something to pop.
a b hash c becomes a, c, and a d hash c also becomes a, c. Equal, true.
Hash hash x: the first two backspaces hit an empty stack and do nothing, then x. That equals x. Good, the guard matters.
O(n plus m) time and space. The backward two-pointer version brings space to O(1).
